strengths: Comprehensive and well-curated dataset with 14,538 training samples spanning multiple modalities (RGB, SAR, GIS, spectral indices) and domains, supported by a systematic curation pipeline with automated validation and deterministic replay verification.

Strong empirical results: OpenEarthAgent (4B) achieves superior tool-order accuracy (67-72%) and argument correctness (62.10% ArgV) compared to larger open-source models, demonstrating effectiveness of targeted training on geospatial reasoning tasks.

Thorough experimental evaluation with step-by-step and end-to-end modes, diverse baselines (GPT-4o, Qwen, Llama, InternLM), multiple metrics (tool accuracy, argument correctness, trajectory fidelity), and detailed error analysis.
Well-designed unified tool registry spanning perceptual, GIS, spectral, and utility operations with modular, extensible architecture and standardized JSON-based interfaces.
Addresses genuine gap in remote sensing: moving from perception-only models to structured, verifiable, interpretable multi-step geospatial reasoning with explicit tool orchestration.

Good presentation with clear figures illustrating framework, reasoning traces, and examples; comprehensive supplementary material with implementation details, error analysis, and evaluation protocols.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core methodology is standard supervised fine-tuning on reasoning trajectories. Main contribution is dataset/application rather than algorithmic innovation, making this primarily a dataset paper rather than a methods contribution suitable for ECCV.

Dataset quality concerns: reasoning traces synthesized via LLM with one-shot prompts; potential biases and quality issues not thoroughly discussed. Manual verification only on test set; no inter-annotator agreement or quality metrics reported for reasoning traces.

Evaluation relies on LLM judges (gpt-4o-mini) for non-generation task accuracy, introducing potential bias and circularity. No out-of-distribution evaluation; all results on curated data with no assessment of generalization to unseen geographies or sensor types.

Missing quantitative comparisons with related geospatial systems (ThinkGeo, Earth-Agent): paper claims to address their limitations but provides no direct performance benchmarking on comparable tasks.

Insufficient analysis of framework design: working memory not formally defined; tool caching strategy not analyzed; no ablation studies on core components; error propagation through multi-step chains not discussed. Extensibility claim (new tools without retraining) unsupported.

Data reproducibility concerns: no explicit dataset release statement; dependency on external services (Nominatim geocoder, GoogleSearch); training on proprietary Qwen3 model. Missing table reference on page 5 indicates incomplete documentation.

Evaluation limitations: generous ±10% tolerance for numerical geospatial measurements; small test set (1,169 samples); unexplained underperformance on summary accuracy compared to GPT-4o; no per-domain or per-reasoning-depth error breakdown.

Tangential to ECCV core interests: work is primarily geospatial/remote sensing application rather than computer vision methodology contribution. Limited discussion of societal impact (e.g., surveillance vs. disaster response applications).

strengths: Comprehensive dataset with 14,538 training + 1,169 test instances spanning seven thematic domains and multiple modalities (RGB, SAR, GIS, spectral indices), with 100K+ reasoning steps
Well-motivated problem addressing genuine gaps in geospatial reasoning: coordinate consistency, scale handling, multispectral analysis, and verifiable outputs
Systematic data curation pipeline with automated validation, quality control, and deterministic replay of reasoning traces
Strong empirical results: OpenEarthAgent-4B achieves 99.51% instance accuracy and 97.18% tool accuracy, substantially outperforming larger open-source models
Extensive baseline comparisons against GPT-4o, Qwen, InternLM, and Llama with both step-by-step and end-to-end evaluation protocols
Unified tool registry design providing standardized abstraction across perceptual, GIS, spectral, and utility operations
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core contribution is standard supervised fine-tuning on reasoning trajectories (Eq. 3), directly replicating established patterns from ReAct and OpenThinkIMG without novel reasoning algorithms, architectures, or learning objectives

Synthetic dataset quality not adequately validated: LLM-generated data, rejection/filtering statistics not reported, no inter-annotator agreement, manual inspection mentioned but not quantified (how many of 1,169 test samples checked?), no assessment of GIS tool reliability

Weak evaluation methodology: (1) No ablation studies isolating which components drive improvements; (2) Answer accuracy assessed via single LLM judge (GPT-4o-mini) without inter-judge agreement or human evaluation; (3) All test data from same distribution as training—no out-of-distribution evaluation; (4) Tool accuracy metrics don't account for partial credit

Insufficient analysis of actual geospatial reasoning: no evidence models understand coordinate systems/projections, no analysis of spatial output consistency (same query → same answer?), no coordinate consistency metrics despite identifying this as key prior work limitation, limited systematic analysis of failure modes beyond aggregate error counts

Reproducibility severely compromised: dataset not released (no mention of public availability), tool implementations unspecified (which GIS libraries?), unresolved references ('Table ??' on p. 5), data generation templates not fully documented, model checkpoints not mentioned, no code release plan

Dataset is primarily a contribution type (Datasets/Benchmarks) not adequately recognized—framed as Algorithms paper but lacks methodological innovation, no release commitment undermines long-term impact

Unfair experimental design: OpenEarthAgent fine-tuned on target data while GPT-4o/o4-mini are not; missing in-context learning baseline (few-shot GPT-4o comparison); model selection justification absent (why 4B over 7B?); training limited to 1 epoch without justification

Geographic and demographic biases not analyzed: data source bias, regional coverage distribution not reported, temporal coverage unclear, potential over-representation of high-income regions likely but unexamined
Incomplete manuscript presentation: reference errors, dense/hard-to-read figures (Fig. 3), inconsistent terminology, limited discussion of limitations and failure modes

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing a genuine gap in the EO community by moving from perception-only to structured geospatial reasoning

Comprehensive and systematic dataset construction with integrated multi-modal pipeline (RGB, SAR, GIS, spectral indices), 14.5K training instances with 100K+ reasoning steps, and rigorous automated validation
Rigorous multi-faceted evaluation with diverse models, step-by-step and end-to-end protocols, and rich metrics showing SOTA tool-use accuracy despite 4B parameter budget
Well-designed extensible framework with unified tool registry, standardized JSON contracts, and tool execution caching enabling composition without retraining
Clear presentation, comprehensive supplementary materials, detailed implementation details supporting reproducibility
Demonstrates practical value with real-world applications and zero-shot reasoning capabilities across diverse geospatial domains

No direct empirical comparison with closely-related work (Earth-Agent, ThinkGeo) despite acknowledging them as closely related; baselines lack fine-tuning on identical data

Extensive synthetic data generation via LLM but insufficient analysis of potential biases, domain shift, and alignment with expert geospatial workflows; no synthetic vs. manual comparison

Evaluation relies on LLM-based judgment (gpt-4o-mini) without inter-rater validation or expert studies; test set from same distribution as training with no out-of-distribution or geographic generalization evaluation
Limited validation of geospatial-specific claims: no coordinate consistency verification, spatial accuracy analysis, or handling of ambiguous spatial references despite centrality to problem
Missing ablation studies on framework components, tool categories, and data source contributions; limited analysis of learned reasoning patterns
Tool execution robustness under-explored: insufficient detail on failure recovery, error propagation, or robustness to malformed inputs
All experiments on single 4B model; unclear scalability to larger models and performance degradation on unseen geographic regions or sensor types

Dataset release status and licensing not discussed, limiting reproducibility and community value; insufficient discussion of failure modes, societal implications, and when human expert review is necessary

strengths: Comprehensive, well-curated multimodal dataset (14.5K train + 1.2K test) spanning 7 domains with 107K reasoning steps and structured thought-action-observation traces—addresses genuine gap in EO reasoning benchmarks

Thoughtfully designed data construction pipeline with multi-stage quality controls (Sample Sufficiency Filter, Annotation Harmonizer, deterministic replay validation) that ensure syntactic correctness and executability
Unified tool registry with standardized JSON-based schema elegantly abstracts heterogeneous geospatial operations (perceptual, GIS, spectral, raster) enabling modular orchestration and extensibility

Rigorous experimental evaluation with dual modes (step-by-step and end-to-end), multiple metrics (Instance/Tool/Argument accuracy, tool-order fidelity), and extensive comparisons across frontier and open-source models

Strong empirical results on tool-use metrics: 4B OpenEarthAgent achieves state-of-the-art syntax/semantics scores (99.51% Inst., 97.18% Tool, 62.10% ArgV) despite small parameter budget, substantially outperforming larger open-source baselines

Comprehensive supplementary material with detailed ablations (data composition, tool schema, in-context learning, tool ordering, high-level planning) and error analysis demonstrating systematic investigation
Commitment to reproducibility via promised public release of code and models, plus extensive tool specifications and evaluation protocols
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: applies standard ReAct-style reasoning and supervised fine-tuning to geospatial domain; tool registry is engineering contribution (standardization) rather than methodological innovation; contribution is integration-focused rather than conceptually advancing tool-augmented reasoning

Data quality concerns insufficiently addressed: queries and reasoning traces are LLM-generated via 'Question Synthesizer'; while validation checks argument correctness, it cannot detect semantic errors in reasoning chains or systematic biases from generative process; 'controlled regeneration and targeted manual verification' is mentioned but never quantified (what % required regeneration? manual verification rate?); no inter-annotator agreement study or human evaluation of reasoning trace quality

Evaluation methodology weaknesses: (1) Answer Accuracy relies on gpt-4o-mini for non-generative tasks; Supplementary S8.1 shows Qwen3-30B assigns systematically higher scores despite preserved rankings, indicating judge-dependent bias; (2) ±10% tolerance threshold for numerical answers lacks justification; (3) despite 'spatially grounded' claims, no explicit coordinate consistency, geometric validity, or GSD-aware correctness metrics; (4) image-generation evaluation only assesses tool-call correctness, not semantic quality of generated imagery

Significant domain-specific performance degradation without analysis: Figure A2 shows 51.9% (urban planning) down to 11.9% (other domains), with aviation/transportation/recreation <25%; paper does not investigate root causes (sparse data? small objects? temporal dynamics?) nor propose targeted solutions, undermining generalization claims

Fairness of comparisons compromised: 4B domain-specialized fine-tuned model vs. general-purpose LLMs conflates model scale with domain alignment; Table A2 shows Qwen3-Instruct + 15 in-context examples reaches 36-45% on multiple metrics, narrowing fine-tuning gap and suggesting specialized training advantage is overstated; no comparisons with EO-specialized VLMs (GeoChat, EarthDial, RemoteCLIP) or other geospatial reasoning frameworks

Missing cross-domain generalization analysis: all train/test splits from same distribution; no evaluation of training on one domain and testing on another to assess transfer; limits evidence for claimed generalization capability

Shallow reasoning depth: average trajectory length ~6.92 (train) and 6.04 (test) steps is relatively short; 'hard' subset only reaches ~7.97 steps average; no analysis of performance scaling with reasoning complexity or planning horizons; unclear how framework handles multi-hop spatial reasoning

Underspecified reasoning trace generation: how are 'thought' steps generated vs. tool invocations? Are thought steps post-hoc explanations or integral? Prompting strategy for 'Question Prompt Suite' and 'Conversational 1-shot Generator' not detailed; consistency enforcement between user intent and generated trajectories not discussed

Absent key ablations: no isolation of dataset contribution vs. agentic framework contribution; no cross-domain generalization study; limited analysis of which tool categories drive performance; no ablation on trace *quality* (correct vs. adversarially perturbed traces)

Limited spatial grounding validation: despite emphasis on 'spatially grounded decision-making,' no evaluation of coordinate drift, geometric validity violations, or spatial consistency beyond tool execution success; GIS tool accuracy (98.52%) may include syntactically-correct but semantically-incorrect spatial operations

strengths: Comprehensive dataset of 14,538 training instances with explicit reasoning traces spanning diverse geospatial domains (urban, environmental, disaster, infrastructure)
Thorough experimental evaluation with dual evaluation modes (step-by-step and end-to-end) and well-designed metrics assessing different reasoning aspects
Extensive ablation studies investigating data composition, tool schema complexity, ordering effects, and planning mechanisms
Strong empirical results showing 4B model achieves competitive performance with larger models (99.51% Inst., 97.18% Tool, 96.08% ArgN. accuracy)
Practical implementation with promised code release and clear tool registry design for standardizing diverse geospatial operations
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: core mechanism is standard ReAct-style reasoning with supervised fine-tuning on execution traces; unified tool registry is primarily an engineering contribution without algorithmic innovation

Unfair baseline comparison: frontier models and open-source LLMs not fine-tuned on this specific task format while OpenEarthAgent is; Table A2 shows in-context learning achieves 89.80% GIS F1, suggesting much improvement is format-specific adaptation
Dataset construction lacks transparency: exact reasoning trajectory generation process unclear, manual verification scope limited to test set, and ground truth validation methodology not detailed

Geospatial correctness not rigorously validated: deterministic replay checks syntax and execution success but provides minimal evidence that results are geographically correct; no validation of coordinate system handling, distance/area accuracy, or spatial operation correctness

Evaluation concerns: Answer Accuracy metric depends on LLM judge (GPT-4o-mini) introducing potential bias (S8.1 shows 5-10% score variation); low ArgV accuracy (62.10%) and modest GIS task performance (55.77%) are concerning for a geospatial reasoning framework; no generalization testing to novel regions or unseen operations

Unclear contribution relative to prior work (Earth-Agent [7] also has GIS+spectral operations; ThinkGeo [29] evaluates tool-augmented EO reasoning); distinguishing contribution is primarily the dataset, which should be clearer

Limited real-world impact validation: examples are relatively simple (distance computation, POI retrieval); no comparison to traditional GIS tools (QGIS, ArcGIS, Google Earth Engine); no user studies demonstrating practical utility

Reproducibility issues: no error bars/confidence intervals or significance testing, single train-test split without cross-validation, many implementation details missing (exact split procedure, annotation QA metrics, LLM synthesis process under-specified)
Marginal fit for ECCV: paper is primarily a dataset/benchmark contribution better suited for specialized remote sensing conferences or dedicated dataset tracks rather than core computer vision venue

Missing failure analysis: Fig. A1 provides limited geospatial-specific error analysis; no investigation of whether reasoning traces contain only successful problem solutions or include educational failures

strengths: Well-motivated problem addressing a genuine gap in EO research: transition from perception-only models to interpretable, tool-driven structured reasoning

High-quality, large-scale dataset with 14,538 training and 1,169 evaluation samples featuring explicit reasoning traces (100K+ reasoning steps) spanning seven geospatial domains with multimodal data (RGB, SAR, GIS, spectral indices)
Well-designed unified tool registry with standardized JSON-based schema elegantly abstracting diverse operators (perceptual, GIS, spectral, raster, utility tools) into extensible interface

Rigorous dual-protocol evaluation combining step-by-step (without tool execution) and end-to-end (with live tool use) assessment with multiple metrics (tool F1, argument accuracy, trajectory fidelity, answer accuracy)

Strong empirical results on procedural metrics despite 4B model size: 62.10 argument value accuracy (vs. 33.55 baseline), 67.75/67.24/72.71 tool-order consistency, balanced performance across tool categories
Comprehensive ablation studies examining data composition, in-context learning, tool schema complexity (5 levels), tool ordering effects, and high-level planning impact
Transparent reproducibility commitment with clear implementation details, public code/model release, and qualitative examples demonstrating real-world capabilities
Systematic evaluation across geospatial domains with domain-stratified performance analysis and cross-benchmark validation on Earth-Agent benchmark
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: core methodology (supervised fine-tuning on reasoning trajectories) is standard practice from prior work (ReAct, OpenThinkIMG, etc.); framework is engineering/dataset contribution rather than methodological advance for ECCV audience

Dataset construction transparency gaps: validation success rates not reported; manual correction percentages unspecified; annotator count, inter-annotator agreement, and systematic reasoning trajectory verification procedures undefined—critical for reproducibility and quality assessment

Evaluation fairness concerns: OpenEarthAgent fine-tuned on reasoning traces while baselines evaluated zero-shot; Table A2 shows in-context learning gains (Qwen3 k=15: 36.44 GIS F1) remain far from fine-tuned model (67.75), suggesting training regime matters more than model; recommend including identically-trained Qwen3-4B baseline

Limited generalization analysis: all evaluation in-domain (OpenEarthAgent dataset and Earth-Agent benchmark); no out-of-distribution tasks, novel tool combinations, or new sensor modalities tested; tool extensibility claimed but not demonstrated during evaluation

Missing critical ablations: no analysis of data efficiency (training set size impact), tool set minimality (essential vs. optional tools), or deterministic replay validation contribution to generalization—directly limiting practical applicability understanding

Insufficient failure mode and limitation discussion: error categorization (S4) lacks insight into failure reasons and conditions; missing discussion of latency, validation cost, privacy, fairness in safety-critical applications (disaster response, infrastructure); brief conclusion limits candid limitation assessment

Statistical rigor gaps: no confidence intervals, standard deviations, or significance tests on results; test set modest (1,169 vs. 14,538 training, 7.4%); unclear whether differences vs. frontier models are statistically meaningful

EO-domain specificity despite generality claims: tool registry features earth-observation-specific tools (GetAreaBoundary, spectral indices NDVI/NBR/NDBI, DisplayOnGeotiff); generalization to other structured reasoning domains unvalidated
